en: OSMONDE : And so?
CLAUDE : That man...
OSMONDE : You do not know him, you have no right to speak of him.
CLAUDE : The mere fact of having given you that letter to read...
OSMONDE : I was the one who demanded it.
CLAUDE : On what terms are you, then?
OSMONDE : I believe he has great affection for me, and I love him very much too.
CLAUDE : But you are no longer a child; you cannot fail to realize that in his feelings for you there is probably something impure.
OSMONDE : You mean physical? I don't doubt it for an instant. (A silence.)
CLAUDE : I remain convinced that if you looked reality in the face, you would understand... To begin with, it is a situation with no way out.
OSMONDE : That is perhaps not absolutely certain.
CLAUDE : You are speculating on his wife's death?
OSMONDE : Oh! That one will bury us all.
CLAUDE : Well then? (A silence.) What do you hope for? What are you counting on?
OSMONDE : I hope for nothing, I count on nothing; I need to see clearly within myself.
CLAUDE : You see, you aren't even sure of what you feel. Thank God for that!

OSMONDE : That is not at all what I mean. What I call seeing clearly within myself is knowing what I, for my part, consider right, and what I consider wrong. (Claude makes a movement.) I have no illusions about the nature of his feelings, and even... perhaps I am going to shock you deeply, but if he had nothing for me but a very respectful friendship, well, I would hardly be pleased... So... No, if I were to commit an indiscretion, I suppose he would be delighted to take advantage of it. All men are the same. (Claude makes a movement.) You, Papa, surely understand that you cannot judge. That indiscretion, all I have to do is not commit it, or else do so with full awareness.
CLAUDE, struggling to control himself : You are speaking completely like a child right now. Or rather, you are trying to deceive yourself. In reality, my poor girl, you are dreadfully distraught.
OSMONDE : Not at all, I assure you.
CLAUDE : Your voice is trembling.
OSMONDE : The day I am certain that there is nothing there but a prejudice...
CLAUDE : Precisely, that day has not come.
OSMONDE : What pleasure can it give you to torment me? Oh! I know very well that it's your calling not to leave people in peace.
CLAUDE : It is my duty to bring you face to face with yourself.
OSMONDE : What do you expect, Papa? To me, that is nothing but a phrase.
CLAUDE : It is my duty to warn you against the sort of vanity—yes, exactly that, vanity—which you feel at the thought that a man harbors an equivocal feeling for you.

OSMONDE : It is not vanity. For the first, and probably the only time in my life, someone is thinking of me without associating me with some vague image of a Christian home and a pious brood. I need to live on my own; the thought of an existence running on rails fills me with horror, and I do not know whether that is a shortcoming. In a life as flat as ours, if one doesn't have the good fortune to believe...
CLAUDE : You imagine it is only a matter of luck?
OSMONDE : Yes; the will has nothing to do with it, I have tried hard enough.

CLAUDE, with mounting bitterness : So one must take this cynicism seriously, this quiet shamelessness. You weigh the pros and cons. Nothing shudders within you at the thought of certain indignities...
OSMONDE : It would not be an indignity.
CLAUDE : When you speak to me of our flat life...

OSMONDE : Every sacrifice that has been asked of me until now has seemed to me derisory, humiliating. Nothing, nothing has changed since the days when I was urged to give the poor children of the parish those holiday gifts I cared for most. And the daily good deed that had to be recorded in the little moleskin notebook. That sort of morality repels me. I grant you that I am on the edge... of a precipice.
CLAUDE : You are intoxicating yourself with the worst kind of literature.
OSMONDE : Literature, Papa, is the suffering of others. It is your immense privilege never to have known certain temptations.
CLAUDE, as if to himself : It is intolerable.
OSMONDE : But that very superiority... it seems to me that it carries a kind of ransom.

CLAUDE : You too! (Abruptly.) Now, listen to me: you claim that life here is too smooth, too easy; you complain of having no task worthy of you. Well then! Since you force me to it, I will disabuse you. To begin with... we are not a family like any other.
OSMONDE : What do you mean?
CLAUDE : It is not a matter of judging anyone, you understand...
OSMONDE : You look so wretched!
CLAUDE, to himself : I cannot bear it.
OSMONDE : Is there something important concerning you that I don't know?

CLAUDE : I had sworn to myself that you would never learn it; and now!... And it will not even have been of my own free will that I told you. (He has stood up and paces back and forth, in the grip of intense agitation.) How I am taken advantage of! How unjust people are!
OSMONDE : How am I taking advantage, Papa?
CLAUDE : I wish everything were over for me.
OSMONDE, bitterly : Since nothing ever ends... for anyone. (A silence.)
CLAUDE : I will have handed down nothing, I will have protected no one, I wonder why I have lived. You are already half corrupted.
OSMONDE, moved : No, surely not.
CLAUDE : Yes, yes, just now you were foreseeing your fall...
OSMONDE : You can prevent everything. First of all by trusting me. That secret, whatever it may be, I want to share it with you.
CLAUDE : You do not know what you are asking.
OSMONDE : I am far braver than you think...
CLAUDE : That is to say, you know nothing of life. Nothing, absolutely nothing. (Abruptly.) Osmonde, I am not your father.
OSMONDE, in astonishment : What are you saying?
CLAUDE : You heard me clearly, I am not your father.
OSMONDE : Then... oh, Papa, am I guessing right? That man who was here the other evening... and who looked at me in such a way...
CLAUDE : Yes.
OSMONDE, with hatred : And her! Oh, I...
CLAUDE, softly : Hush!
OSMONDE : Papa! (She is in tears; Claude holds her tight against his heart.) My head is spinning.
CLAUDE : My poor darling, I ask your forgiveness.
OSMONDE : No...
CLAUDE : I should never have told you.
OSMONDE : It will pass... I have to get used to it...
CLAUDE : My poor child!
OSMONDE : Only... you will explain to me... I have the right to know everything.
CLAUDE : My darling, it is a dreadful story, you do not need to know the details. You must not question... anyone, believe me. It would be a pointless cruelty.
OSMONDE : And I imagined I had a family.
CLAUDE : You must look at things from above... (Osmonde looks at him.) You have been dearly loved.
OSMONDE : Loved by you.
CLAUDE : By both of us. (Osmonde makes a movement.) This misfortune has never weighed upon your life.
OSMONDE : You think so? I, for my part, realize now...
CLAUDE : And even now that I have had to reveal it to you.
OSMONDE, with veiled surprise : You mean that nothing will have changed...
CLAUDE : My darling, understand me, I am not asking the impossible, but what I have the right to require of you...
OSMONDE : Well?
CLAUDE : Is that you forbid yourself from passing certain judgments.
OSMONDE : But listen, one is not the master of one's thoughts.
CLAUDE : Up to a certain point, nonetheless. After all, think... it would be revolting.

OSMONDE : And besides... it is very strange, but deep down, it is as though this were not a discovery... You tell me one must not judge Mama, but I feel very well that I have always judged her. Her virtues, her goodness, her charity, her austerity—I was never taken in by them. It is as if I had realized that none of that was her. Her—why, that was the expression she has when she catches you in the wrong, or else...
CLAUDE : You are causing me dreadful pain. I cannot bear to hear you speak of your mother like that.
OSMONDE : So we must go on pretending, even when it is just the two of us?
CLAUDE : You owe your mother respect.
OSMONDE : Do you want me to tell you? It is more like a relief that I feel. Before, I didn't quite dare admit to myself that I...
CLAUDE : That you...

OSMONDE : Now I will dare... (A silence.) Only, oh, Papa! If everything had come to light back then, if there had been a scandal, if she had been forced to leave and you had kept me with you... after all, that could easily have happened... how happy we two could have been!
CLAUDE : Osmonde!

OSMONDE : Everything would have been as though she had died... simply. It isn't always a misfortune when someone dies in a family. You are so generous! You would have spoken to me of her, and I would have believed she was someone worth mourning.
CLAUDE : But what you are saying is appalling!

OSMONDE : Now, it is true that you might perhaps have been too generous. You wouldn't have wanted to separate me from her; good heavens! as if... or else, you would have held her back; you always believe that people can be saved in spite of themselves. Yes, who knows if you wouldn't have forgiven her? And one would always have wondered... Fortunately, that didn't happen; did it? That isn't how things took place, is it?
CLAUDE, with effort : No, things did not happen that way.

OSMONDE : So much the better. If I had to think you had been playing a part for twenty years... it would spoil even your tenderness for me. Papa, I hurt you earlier, I seemed to be thinking only of myself, but I love you very much, you know, and now that this secret exists between us...
CLAUDE : No, no, I was wrong. You are only a child who has pity for no one... (With a kind of desperate fervor.) My little Osmonde, you must swear to me that these horrible ideas will never return.
OSMONDE : What ideas?
CLAUDE : If I had to lose you like that... Why are you smiling?
OSMONDE : One would think you were trying to take advantage... But I understand. You are still bruised all over, still sick at heart...
OSMONDE : When you think that ten days ago... twelve days ago, you didn't know...
CLAUDE, in a low voice, as if with shame : No, I didn't know.
OSMONDE : Poor, darling Papa. (She kisses him.)
[SCENE VIII]
THE SAME, MME LEMOYNE
MME LEMOYNE, touched : Ah, how sweet that is. Good day, darling. Tell me, Claude, I am so pleased with what Francis just told me.
OSMONDE : What is that, Grandmother?

MME LEMOYNE : I thought your papa was looking so unwell that I asked Uncle Francis to drop by to see him. Fortunately, it seems it is nothing at all. (To Claude.) You look as though your eyes are red?
OSMONDE : It's a speck of dust.

MME LEMOYNE : Above all, don't rub, that only inflames it more... (To Osmonde.) My little darling, your mama sends word that she needs you urgently... I believe it has to do with a shopping list for Christmas.
OSMONDE : Mama has no need of my advice, I guarantee you it will be quickly dispatched; see you shortly, Grandmother... (She exits.)
[SCENE IX]
MME LEMOYNE : Guess what Madame Hourseau just told me.
CLAUDE : How do you expect me to know?
MME LEMOYNE : They are on the verge of sounding you out for a major parish on the Right Bank... Chaillot.
CLAUDE : You know I don't want to hear of it.
MME LEMOYNE : It seems the proposal will be made to you in such flattering terms...
CLAUDE : I am not in the habit of having my hand forced. The day I leave the Rue d'Alésia...
MME LEMOYNE : Well?
CLAUDE : It won't be to go to the Avenue Marceau.
MME LEMOYNE : My dear child, it is not for me to give you advice, but I cannot understand how you have no desire to address an audience more worthy of you.
CLAUDE : It isn't a question of an audience.
MME LEMOYNE : I am not the only one who thinks that with your eloquence...
CLAUDE : I am not a lecturer.
MME LEMOYNE : Your poor father always used to say: "Our place is wherever we can be of the greatest service."
CLAUDE : Agreed.
MME LEMOYNE : Madame Hourseau was telling me again just now that many people who would be glad to hear you are frightened by the distance.
CLAUDE : There are trams, and the metro is five minutes away...
MME LEMOYNE : People you could do good to, intellectuals. (Claude makes a movement.) Surely it isn't for me to tell you how absorbing Parisian life is.
CLAUDE : Those people's time is too precious.
CLAUDE, abruptly : Besides, I may soon have some news to announce to you, real news.
MME LEMOYNE, with excitement : You are returning to your thesis on Melanchthon... Claude, what joy!
CLAUDE : There is no question of that...
MME LEMOYNE : That is a pity!
CLAUDE : It concerns my ministry. As I am unfortunately far less sure than you are of my evangelical gifts, or even... (He stops.)
MME LEMOYNE : But what are you saying?
CLAUDE, as if to himself : I have had enough, I have had enough...
MME LEMOYNE : I am truly afraid that Francis did not examine you properly.
CLAUDE : That is a little too convenient... besides, yes, you are right, I am ill, mortally ill.
MME LEMOYNE : Good heavens!
CLAUDE : Don't worry, it is only my conscience that is ill.
MME LEMOYNE : You gave me such a fright, Claude... when I still get breathless so easily!
CLAUDE : Whether I die of sorrow and disgust with myself, what does that matter so long as my digestion is good... Listen: just now, I lied ignobly, do you hear me?
MME LEMOYNE : I am quite sure that is only a figure of speech.
CLAUDE : That's it, pour me some nice hot herbal tea, completely bland, just like when I was ten years old... Oh, Mother, I resent you too.
MME LEMOYNE : You have led the life of a great Christian.
CLAUDE : First I should have led the life of a man, and I am not a man; I didn't even know how to love like a man—or hate like a man.
MME LEMOYNE : Hate?
CLAUDE : Yes, yes, hate too... I am nothing, I am nothing. (He collapses into an armchair.)
[SCENE X]
THE SAME, EDMÉE
EDMÉE, having pushed the door ajar : What is going on?
MME LEMOYNE : He is quite ill. We absolutely must consult a doctor. You should let me take him to Lausanne. We have very good specialists...
EDMÉE : In what?
MME LEMOYNE : In everything, in everything...
CLAUDE, harshly : What are the two of you plotting there? Ah yes, you may well look at me... I am your handiwork.
